source.title: Considerations for the Regulation of Generative AI-Enabled Medical Devices: Discussion Paper and Request for Feedback
source.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Digital Health Center of Excellence
source.question_text_note: question_text must hold the exact wording from the discussion paper. Run scripts/fetch_fda_questions.py to import it from the PDF. While question_text is empty, the site shows a pending notice and links to the source instead of paraphrasing.

questions.short_title: Characterizing risk when outputs vary run to run
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how risk should be characterized for devices whose output is not deterministic.
questions.about: Existing risk frameworks assume a fixed output for a fixed input. A generative system can produce a different answer to the same question twice, which makes the unit of risk harder to define: the model, the response, or the pattern of responses over a population of uses.

questions.short_title: Intended use boundaries for conversational systems
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how intended use should be defined when a system responds to open-ended user input.
FDA asks whether output categories should drive different regulatory treatment.
FDA asks how the presence or absence of a clinician intermediary should affect risk.

questions.short_title: Estimating severity and probability of harm
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how harm probability should be estimated for open-ended outputs.
FDA asks what mitigations should be expected and how their effectiveness should be shown.

questions.short_title: Evidence expectations and the competency-based approach
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks whether a competency-based premarket approach is appropriate and what evidence should be expected at each level of risk.
questions.about: The paper suggests evidence should scale with risk, but does not say what the floor is. Commenters read the same sentence very differently depending on whether they are funding the studies or relying on them.

questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how sponsors should choose and disclose benchmarks.
FDA asks what study designs are appropriate for generative outputs.
FDA asks how sponsors should show that non-clinical benchmarks are valid and reflect the intended population.
FDA asks how sponsors should select and justify a clinical confirmation approach, from retrospective review to prospective study.
FDA asks how sample sizes should be justified and what adversarial testing should be expected before market.

questions.short_title: Human factors and human-AI team performance
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how human factors evaluation should account for interaction with generative output.
questions.about: The clinically relevant unit of performance is often the clinician plus the tool, not the model alone. Commenters split on whether FDA can meaningfully regulate a combined system whose human half varies by site.

questions.short_title: Transparency and labeling for generative output
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks what users should be told about how output is produced.
FDA asks what technical documentation should accompany a submission.
FDA asks how reliance on an external base model should be disclosed.
FDA asks how ground truth should be established where expert judgement varies.

questions.short_title: Trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks under what conditions greater premarket uncertainty could be accepted in exchange for stronger postmarket monitoring.
questions.about: The paper floats a trade: less evidence before market if monitoring after market is strong enough. Whether that trade is attractive depends on who runs the monitoring, what it costs, and what happens when it finds something.

questions.short_title: Who is responsible for ongoing monitoring
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how monitoring responsibility should be allocated across the deployment chain.
questions.about: Monitoring requires data the manufacturer usually cannot see and interpretation the health system usually cannot fund. The paper assumes a responsible party without naming one.

questions.short_title: Drift detection and machine-based supervisory monitoring
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how performance drift should be detected, what should trigger action, and whether machine-based supervisory agents could run monitoring functions.
FDA asks how updates to a generative model should be managed after clearance.
questions.about: Change control assumes discrete, sponsor-initiated versions. Generative products change through prompts, retrieval content, tool access, and upstream base-model updates the sponsor did not schedule.

questions.summary_ask: FDA asks what belongs in a predetermined change control plan for these products.

questions.short_title: Adverse event reporting for generative outputs
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks what constitutes a reportable event when the output is text.

questions.short_title: Local deployment assurance and site configuration
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how site-level configuration and upstream model updates should be accounted for in ongoing assurance.
questions.about: The same cleared product behaves differently depending on EHR configuration, retrieval content, patient population, and which safeguards the site turns on. Little of that is visible in the submission.

questions.short_title: Foundation model suppliers and master files
questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how reliance on third-party foundation models should be handled, including whether voluntary Foundation Model Master Files would be practical and useful.
questions.about: A regulated product can change behavior because a supplier shipped a new checkpoint. Supplier controls in the quality system were written for components, not for models that update on a commercial schedule.

questions.summary_ask: FDA asks how systems that take actions, not just produce text, should be evaluated.
questions.about: Once a system can place an order, send a message, or trigger a workflow, the regulatory question shifts from output quality to how far an error can travel before a person intervenes.
